summary: Explains the general ways other protocols and applications can use Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) to learn quickly that a path has failed. It sets out how a client protocol, such as a routing protocol, can rely on BFD for fast failure detection. It is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: A smoke alarm tells everyone in the house about a fire fast. This document explains how different programs can use a quick-warning helper to learn that a connection has broken.

subtitle: How routing protocols and other network functions should use BFD's fast failure signal without letting it run their lives.

tldr.problem: Many network functions need to learn quickly that a path has failed, but their own liveness checks are too slow, unsuitable or missing. Writing a separate BFD document for each one would take a long series of short documents.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5882 describes in general terms how a client such as a routing protocol supplies session parameters to BFD, receives session state back, and reacts using its own existing mechanisms. BFD acts only as an advisory service.
tldr.outcome: Because clients react with mechanisms they already have, BFD use has essentially no interoperability issues, and one system can use BFD even if its neighbor does not.

facts.label: BFD sessions per data protocol path

today: RFC 5882 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the general companion to the BFD protocol in RFC 5880.

sections.title: BFD as an Advisory Service
sections.content:
The BFD protocol has one job: verify connectivity between a pair of systems, for a particular data protocol, across a path of any technology, length or OSI layer. How quickly a failure is noticed can be tuned by trading protocol overhead and system load against detection time.

BFD is not meant to report control protocol liveness. Instead, a client supplies session parameters (neighbor address, time parameters, protocol options) and BFD returns the session state, where the Up transitions matter most. BFD has no discovery mechanism, so the application must bootstrap the session.

An implementation SHOULD set up only a single BFD session per data protocol path, however many applications use it. If applications ask for different parameters, resolving that is a local matter, and BFD notifies all bound applications of a state change.

BFD does not carry application-specific information, partly because its latency can be unpredictable and so it is a poor transport. Since clients use their own mechanisms to react, BFD may even interact with only one of a pair of systems without ill effect.
sections.eli5: BFD just says whether the road is open or closed. Each program decides for itself what to do, and BFD never carries messages for them.

sections.title: Session State and Clients
sections.content:
How a BFD session talks to its clients is mostly an implementation matter, but the RFC suggests an adaptation layer between the BFD state machine and the clients. It describes three behaviors.

Hysteresis. An implementation may hide rapid Up/Down/Up changes, which helps with process restarts. A system MAY skip notifying clients if the session drops and returns to Up within a reasonable period (the length is out of scope). If it does not return in time, clients SHOULD be told of the failure.

AdminDown. This state means the session was taken down on purpose and says nothing about the data path. A system SHOULD NOT report a connectivity failure if the local or remote state goes to AdminDown, as long as the client has independent liveness detection. A client with none SHOULD be told of a failure, treating AdminDown like Down.

Hitless establishment. Bringing up or re-establishing a BFD session, for example after a process restart, SHOULD NOT cause a connectivity failure notification to clients.
sections.eli5: If the lookout blinks for a second, you may not need to panic. If the lookout says they are just going on a break, that is not a blocked road either.

sections.title: Working with Control Protocols
sections.content:
Routing protocols are the most common clients. The aim is to tell the control protocol whether the data protocol can get through, so traffic can be rerouted faster than the protocol's native detection allows.

Adjacency establishment. If either session state is AdminDown, a control protocol adjacency MUST be allowed. Establishment SHOULD be blocked if both systems are willing to run BFD but a session cannot be established, but SHOULD NOT be blocked if the neighbor is believed not to support BFD. Willingness can be signaled explicitly by the control protocol. On LANs, blocking on only a subset of systems may break the control protocol's assumption of full connectivity.

Reacting to Up to Down. A protocol with a single data protocol SHOULD act so traffic no longer goes to the failing path, using an explicit path-state mechanism if it has one, and otherwise emulating a control protocol timeout for that neighbor. With multiple data protocols and a shared topology, the path is treated as failed for all of them, otherwise traffic for the failed protocol would be black-holed. With independent topologies, only the failed data protocol is rerouted.

Multiple control protocols. All of them MUST share one BFD session to the same remote system for the same data protocol. When protocols depend on each other, such as OSPF and IBGP, it is best for the one lowest in the hierarchy to use BFD, because the cost of a BGP peer state transition is high.
sections.eli5: When the lookout says the road is blocked, the driver takes another road. If several drivers are on the same road, they share one lookout.

sections.title: Graceful Restart Interactions
sections.content:
Graceful Restart mechanisms (for IS-IS, OSPF and BGP) let a control protocol restart without making the system look failed, on the assumption that a separate forwarding plane keeps working. BFD announces through the Control Plane Independent C bit whether it shares fate with the control plane.

If the C bit is set in both directions, BFD does not share fate with the control plane, so a BFD failure means data cannot be forwarded. Any Graceful Restart in progress SHOULD be aborted and a topology change signaled.

If the C bit is clear in either direction, the BFD failure may be just a side effect of the restart. It is best not to abort the Graceful Restart, with the risk that a simultaneous forwarding plane failure goes unnoticed. If the control protocol can signal a planned restart, the restart SHOULD NOT be aborted.

Protocols that cannot signal a planned restart depend on the restarted system entering Graceful Restart before the adjacency times out. A system MAY lengthen its BFD Detection Time beyond the control protocol's restart period beforehand, and SHOULD NOT send BFD Control packets until neighbors probably know a restart is under way, because the first packet will make the BFD session fail.
sections.eli5: If a driver stops for a planned pit stop, the lookout should not scream that the car has crashed. Whether to listen depends on whether the lookout can see the road separately from the driver.

sections.title: Other Uses, Layers and Planned Outages
sections.content:
BFD can also drive non-protocol functions. For example, if the remote system is known or presumed to be BFD capable and the session is not Up, a static route SHOULD be withdrawn; if it is believed not to support BFD, that SHOULD NOT be done. Without a protocol, sessions are bootstrapped from configuration, and endpoints and discriminators come from configuration too.

BFD protects a single data protocol and is encapsulated in it. IPv4 and IPv6 over the same link are two paths and need two sessions, and one session can be run per differentiated services level, with BFD Control packets marked like the data packets.

For bundles of parallel links, the RFC gives example approaches: run BFD only at layer N (complete decoupling), let layer N-1 give hints so the BFD session fails faster, aggregate BFD sessions run on each layer N-1 link, or combine these.

For tunnels and pseudowires, running BFD inside the tunnel is recommended. Before a planned outage, or before deconfiguring BFD, a system SHOULD go to AdminDown for at least one Detection Time so the remote side knows it is deliberate; simply stopping packets would be seen as a failure.
sections.eli5: Each kind of road needs its own lookout. Before closing a road on purpose, tell the lookout first so nobody panics.

sections.title: Interoperability and Protocol Examples
sections.content:
BFD always interoperates at a basic level, since asynchronous mode is mandatory and other modes are negotiated at run time. Interaction with clients is loosely coupled, so problems are very unlikely unless BFD is applied in contradictory ways. At worst, BFD advising only one side gives asymmetric failure detection.

Section 10 of the RFC is non-normative and gives examples. OSPF and IS-IS have Hello protocols whose minimum detection time is two seconds for OSPF and one second for IS-IS; BFD can give arbitrarily small times. After a BFD failure, OSPF neighbors are torn down, and IS-IS uses topology-specific advertising or simulates an adjacency failure. OSPF Virtual Links MUST use the multihop mechanism of RFC 5883, and BFD authentication SHOULD be used.

For BGP, EBGP sessions may use one-hop (RFC 5881) or multihop BFD, but IBGP generally should not if the IGP already does. For RIP, a BFD failure simulates expiry of the timeout timer for routes from that neighbor; routes with a different next hop may otherwise linger for 180 seconds.
sections.eli5: The lookout works the same for every kind of driver, so everyone can understand the warning, though each driver reacts in their own way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says it raises no additional security issues beyond those of the specifications in its normative references. In the protocol examples it does encourage BFD authentication for OSPF Virtual Links and for BGP.
sections.eli5: This document adds no new locks, but it suggests using the existing ones in risky places.

items.title: Advisory only
items.text: BFD informs clients, who react with their own mechanisms.

items.title: One session per path
items.text: Applications share a single session per data protocol path.

items.title: No discovery
items.text: The application bootstraps the BFD session.

items.title: Carries nothing else
items.text: No application-specific data is carried in BFD.
